**Solution.** We claim the unique solution is $f(x) = 4x$.

**Verification.** $f(f(xy)+2xy) = f(4xy+2xy) = f(6xy) = 24xy$, and $3xf(y)+3yf(x) = 3x\cdot 4y + 3y\cdot 4x = 24xy$. ✓

**Uniqueness.** Let $P(x,y)$ denote the assertion. The left-hand side $f(f(xy)+2xy)$ depends only on the product $xy$, hence so does the right-hand side $3(xf(y)+yf(x))$. Therefore $xf(y)+yf(x)$ depends only on $xy$. Dividing by $xy>0$,

$$\frac{f(x)}{x} + \frac{f(y)}{y} \text{ depends only on } xy.$$

Set $h(t) = f(t)/t$ and $a = f(1) = h(1)$. There exists $G$ with $h(x)+h(y) = G(xy)$. Taking $y=1$: $G(x) = h(x)+a$, so

$$h(x)+h(y) = h(xy)+a, \qquad\text{i.e.,}\quad h(xy)=h(x)+h(y)-a.$$

Define $k(t) = h(t) - a$. Then $k(1)=0$ and

$$k(xy) = k(x)+k(y) \quad\text{for all } x,y>0. \tag{1}$$

Since $f(t) = t\,h(t) = t(a+k(t)) > 0$ for all $t>0$, we have $a+k(t)>0$, i.e. $k(t)>-a$ for all $t>0$. Also $f(t)+2t = t(a+k(t)+2) > 0$ gives the stronger bound

$$k(t) > -(a+2) \quad\text{for all } t>0. \tag{2}$$

Now substitute $f(t)=t(a+k(t))$ into the original equation. With $u=xy$ and $K:=k(u)=k(x)+k(y)$,

$$f(xy)+2xy = u\bigl(a+K+2\bigr) =: t.$$

Using (1), $k(t)=k(u)+k(a+K+2)=K+k(a+K+2)$ (note $a+K+2 = t/u > 0$, so it lies in the domain). The equation $f(t)=3u(2a+K)$ becomes

$$u(a+K+2)\bigl(a+K+k(a+K+2)\bigr) = 3u(2a+K).$$

Setting $B := a+K+2$ (so $a+K = B-2$ and $2a+K = a+B-2$),

$$B\bigl(B-2+k(B)\bigr) = 3(a+B-2),$$

hence

$$k(B) = -B + 5 + \frac{3a-6}{B}. \tag{3}$$

This holds for every $B$ in the set $S:=\{a+k(u)+2 : u>0\}\subseteq(0,\infty)$ (the inclusion follows from (2)).

**Claim:** $k\equiv 0$. Suppose not. Writing $k(e^s)=A(s)$ for an additive function $A:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ (i.e. $A(s+t)=A(s)+A(t)$), nontriviality of $k$ means $A$ is nontrivial. Pick any Hamel-basis element $e_0$ with $A(e_0)=c\neq 0$; then $A(q\,e_0)=qc$ for all $q\in\mathbb Q$, so $\operatorname{im}(A)\supseteq c\mathbb Q$, which is unbounded below. Thus $\operatorname{im}(k)$ is unbounded below, contradicting (2). Therefore $k\equiv 0$.

With $k\equiv 0$, we have $f(t)=at$, and the original equation gives $a(a+2)=6a$, i.e. $a(a-4)=0$. Since $a>0$, $a=4$.

Therefore $f(x) = 4x$ for all $x>0$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
